newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Wool prices outperform cotton, polyester-IWS.
newsitem.headline: Wool prices outperform cotton, polyester-IWS.

text.p: Wool prices fared better in 1996 than other textile fibres, breaking the trend seen since 1994, the International Wool Secretariat (IWS) said in its monthly market briefing.
This had been particularly so for fine wool, it said.
The synthetic fibre market continued to be depressed by excess global capacity. Many synthetic fibre producers remained under pressure and had cut back operating levels, it said.
Expectations for a good cotton crop in 1996/97, combined with cautious hand-to-mouth buying by spinners, had resulted in falling cotton prices in 1996, IWS said.
Fine wool prices had increased as fine wool supply tightened and demand from traditional markets, particularly Japan, improved, the IWS said.
This trend was expected to continue with improved fine wool prices and continued lower prices for polyester and cotton forecast, it said.
IWS also said the sales value of wool apparel rose in China in the first six months of 1996, a survey of 100 department stores showed.
Expenditure on clothing in China was rising steadily, with retail sales in the first half of 1996 growing at about 14 percent year-on-year on an inflation-adjusted basis.
Exports of wool textiles and clothing, however, fell in the first half of 1996.
China's output5 of yarn, fabric and apparel in the first five months of 1996 was five to eight percent higher than in the same period of 1995, with demand driven by the domestic market, IWS said.
Some flattening off in growth was occurring although apparel production was holding up better than yarn and fabric production, it said.
China's total raw wool and top imports fell by nine percent in the first seven months of 1996 compared with a year earlier, the briefing said.
Imports from Australia were up by 15 percent but imports from Uruguay, South Africa and the former Soviet Union were all down.

On the Indian market, IWS said the market for wool and wool blend fabrics had stagnated because of political uncertainty associated with the general election in May and a shift of purchase priorities among upper and middle class consumers.
The lull was expected to be temporary, with a recovery expected before the new year, it said.
The export market for Indian wool products was performing well, with the value of exports rising by 13 percent to 42 percent for selected wool products in 1995/96 on an inflation-adjusted basis.
